testName: IISER IAT - Diversity in the Living World (20 Questions) - Version 2

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: According to the rules of binomial nomenclature, which of the following is INCORRECT regarding the scientific name of an organism?
options: The generic name begins with a capital letter
The specific epithet begins with a small letter
Both names should be underlined when handwritten
The scientific name can be followed by the name of any taxonomist who worked on it
questions.explanation:
Step 1: According to ICBN rules, scientific names must follow strict conventions: Generic name capitalized, specific epithet lowercase, both underlined/italicized, and followed by the original author's name (the one who first validly published the name), not just any taxonomist.
Step 2: Option D is incorrect because only the original describer's name (authority) is cited, not any subsequent worker.
Why others are wrong: (A), (B), and (C) are all correct rules of binomial nomenclature.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The sequence of taxonomic categories in descending order is:
options: Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
Kingdom → Division → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
Kingdom → Phylum → Order → Class → Family → Genus → Species
Kingdom → Class → Phylum → Order → Family → Genus → Species
questions.explanation:
Step 1: The standard taxonomic hierarchy from highest to lowest rank is: Kingdom → Phylum (or Division in plants) → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species.
Step 2: Option A shows the correct sequence used for animals and most organisms.
Why others are wrong: (B) Division is used for plants, not the standard animal sequence; (C) Order and Class are reversed; (D) Class and Phylum are reversed.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of Kingdom Monera?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Kingdom Monera includes all prokaryotes (bacteria and cyanobacteria).
Step 2: Key features: No membrane-bound nucleus (nucleoid region), no membrane-bound organelles, cell wall with peptidoglycan, reproduce by binary fission.
Step 3: Option C states 'Membrane-bound nucleus and organelles present' - this is the defining feature of eukaryotes, not prokaryotes.
Why others are wrong: (A), (B), and (D) are all correct characteristics of Monera.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A student observes a unicellular organism that is eukaryotic, photosynthetic, has a cell wall made of cellulose, and possesses two flagella of unequal length. This organism belongs to:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze the characteristics: Eukaryotic + Photosynthetic + Cellulose cell wall + Two unequal flagella.
Step 2: Dinoflagellates are characterized by having two flagella of unequal length (transverse and longitudinal) that lie in perpendicular grooves, cellulose plates in cell wall, and are photosynthetic.
Why others are wrong: (A) Euglenoids have protein pellicle, no cellulose wall, one or two equal flagella; (C) Diatoms have silica frustules, no flagella in vegetative state; (D) Slime moulds are saprophytic, lack cell walls during vegetative phase.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Refer to the phylogenetic tree diagram showing evolutionary relationships among major plant groups. Which node represents the first appearance of vascular tissue (xylem and phloem)?
options: Node B (at the base of all land plants)
Node D (at the divergence of Gymnosperms and Angiosperms)
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Vascular tissue (xylem and phloem) first evolved in the lineage leading to vascular plants (tracheophytes), after the divergence of non-vascular plants (bryophytes).
Step 2: Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) lack true vascular tissue.
Step 3: Pteridophytes (ferns and allies) were the first true vascular plants.
Why others are wrong: (B) Base of land plants includes bryophytes which lack vascular tissue; (C) After pteridophytes is too late - they already have it; (D) Gymnosperms and angiosperms are both seed plants that already had vascular tissue from earlier ancestors.
questions.imagePrompt: A phylogenetic tree diagram showing evolutionary relationships among plant groups. Root at left, branches extending right. Labels: Algae (outgroup), then Bryophytes branching off, then Node A leading to Pteridophytes, then Node C leading to Gymnosperms and Angiosperms (Node D). Node B at base of land plant clade. Arrows indicating evolutionary traits: vascular tissue, seeds, flowers. Clean cladogram style with labeled nodes A, B, C, D.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about viruses is CORRECT?
options: Viruses are cellular entities that can reproduce independently outside host cells
All viruses contain both DNA and RNA as genetic material
Viruses are considered as intermediate between living and non-living because they show metabolic activity outside host cells
Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites that can only replicate inside living host cells
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze each statement:
(A) FALSE - Viruses are acellular (not cellular) and cannot reproduce independently.
(B) FALSE - Viruses contain either DNA OR RNA, never both simultaneously.
(C) FALSE - Viruses show no metabolic activity outside host cells; they are inert particles.
(D) TRUE - Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites - can only replicate inside living host cells using host machinery.
Step 2: Only statement D is correct.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question:
The cell wall composition differs across kingdoms. Match the kingdom with its characteristic cell wall material:

Column I (Kingdom)    Column II (Cell Wall Material)
a) Monera        (i) Cellulose
b) Fungi         (ii) Peptidoglycan
c) Plantae        (iii) Chitin
d) Protista (Diatoms)   (iv) Silica

Select the correct match:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Match each kingdom to its cell wall composition:
a) Monera (Bacteria) - Peptidoglycan (murein) (match ii)
b) Fungi - Chitin (nitrogenous polysaccharide) (match iii)
c) Plantae - Cellulose (polysaccharide of glucose units) (match i)
d) Protista (Diatoms specifically) - Silica (siliceous frustules) (match iv)
Step 2: Correct combination: a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
Why others are wrong: All other combinations mismatch fundamental cell wall biochemistry across kingdoms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A plant specimen shows the following characteristics: thalloid body, no true roots/stems/leaves, rhizoids present, no vascular tissue, alternation of generations with independent gametophyte and sporophyte attached to gametophyte. This specimen belongs to:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze the characteristics:
• Thalloid body, no true roots/stems/leaves - non-vascular plant
• Rhizoids (not true roots) - characteristic of bryophytes
• No vascular tissue - eliminates pteridophytes and gymnosperms
• Independent gametophyte, sporophyte attached to gametophyte - unique bryophyte feature
Step 2: These are defining characteristics of Bryophyta (mosses, liverworts, hornworts).
Why others are wrong: (A) Algae are aquatic, don't have rhizoids or this life cycle; (C) Pteridophytes have vascular tissue and true roots; (D) Gymnosperms have vascular tissue, seeds, and independent sporophyte.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The diagram shows the life cycle of a typical pteridophyte. Identify the stage labeled 'X' that represents the independent, photosynthetic, haploid stage producing gametes.
options: Young sporophyte embryo developing from zygote
questions.explanation:
Step 1: In pteridophytes, there is alternation of generations with distinct haploid and diploid phases.
Step 2: The gametophyte (n) is the independent, photosynthetic, haploid stage called prothallus - a small, heart-shaped structure that produces male (antheridia) and female (archegonia) gametangia.
Step 3: The sporophyte (2n) is the dominant, visible fern plant.
Why others are wrong: (A) Sporophyte is diploid (2n), not haploid; (C) Spore mother cell is diploid, not independent stage; (D) Embryo is diploid and dependent, not independent.
questions.imagePrompt: A diagram showing the life cycle of a fern (pteridophyte). Circular flow with arrows: Large fern plant (sporophyte, 2n) → sporangia on underside of fronds → meiosis → spores (n) → germination → small heart-shaped structure labeled 'X' (prothallus/gametophyte, n) showing rhizoids, antheridia (male), archegonia (female) → fertilization → zygote (2n) → young embryo → mature sporophyte. Label 'X' clearly indicated with pointer. Botanical illustration style.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of angiosperms but NOT found in gymnosperms?
options: Presence of vascular tissue (xylem and phloem)
Double fertilization resulting in formation of endosperm
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Compare angiosperms and gymnosperms:
• Both have vascular tissue (A) - present in both
• Both produce seeds (C) - defining feature of spermatophytes
• Both produce pollen (D) - male gametophyte in seed plants
• Double fertilization - one sperm fertilizes egg to form zygote, other fuses with polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm - this is unique to angiosperms.
Step 2: In gymnosperms, endosperm is haploid (female gametophyte tissue) and formed before fertilization.
Why others are wrong: (A), (C), and (D) are features shared by both angiosperms and gymnosperms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A lichen is an example of which type of ecological association?
options: Parasitism where fungus harms the algal partner
Commensalism where fungus benefits and alga is unaffected
Mutualism where both fungal and algal (or cyanobacterial) partners benefit
Predation where fungus consumes the algal partner
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Lichens are composite organisms consisting of a fungus (mycobiont) and a photosynthetic partner (photobiont - algae or cyanobacteria).
Step 2: This is a classic example of mutualism:
• Fungus provides shelter, absorbs water and minerals, protects from harsh conditions
• Alga/Cyanobacterium performs photosynthesis, provides organic carbon food
• Both partners benefit and cannot survive independently in the lichen habitat
Why others are wrong: (A) Not parasitism - neither is harmed; (B) Not commensalism - alga also benefits; (D) Not predation - alga is not consumed, it lives and photosynthesizes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about prions is INCORRECT?
options: Prions contain protein only and lack nucleic acids (DNA or RNA)
Prions cause neurodegenerative diseases like Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
Prions can be destroyed by standard sterilization methods that destroy nucleic acids
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Prions (Proteinaceous Infectious Particles) are:
• Abnormally folded proteins (PrP^Sc) that induce normal proteins (PrP^C) to misfold
• Contain no nucleic acids (DNA or RNA) - unique among infectious agents
• Cause transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (BSE/mad cow disease, CJD, kuru)
• Extremely resistant to heat, radiation, and standard sterilization
Step 2: Statement D is INCORRECT - prions are NOT destroyed by standard sterilization (autoclaving, UV, nucleases) because they lack nucleic acids. They require extreme methods (proteases, very high heat, strong chemicals).
Why others are wrong: (A), (B), and (C) are all correct statements about prions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The table below compares characteristics of different animal phyla. Identify the phylum that shows: triploblastic development, bilateral symmetry, pseudocoelomate body cavity, and complete digestive tract with mouth and anus.
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze the combination of characteristics:
• Triploblastic - three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm)
• Bilateral symmetry - single plane divides body into mirror halves
• Pseudocoelomate - false body cavity (blastocoel not completely lined by mesoderm)
• Complete digestive tract - separate mouth and anus
Step 2: Nematoda (Aschelminthes/roundworms) uniquely possess all these features together.
Why others are wrong: (A) Platyhelminthes are acoelomate (no body cavity), incomplete digestive tract; (C) Annelida are true coelomates (eucoelomates); (D) Arthropoda are true coelomates with haemocoel.
questions.imagePrompt: A comparison table with four columns: Phylum, Germ Layers (Diploblastic/Triploblastic), Body Cavity (Acoelomate/Pseudocoelomate/Coelomate), Digestive Tract (Complete/Incomplete). Rows for Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Arthropoda. Some cells filled, others blank for interpretation. Clean scientific table format.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which characteristic distinguishes chordates from all other animal phyla?
options: Presence of bilateral symmetry and triploblastic development
Presence of notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, and pharyngeal slits at some life stage
Presence of segmented body and appendages
Presence of deuterostome mode of development
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze each option:
(A) Bilateral symmetry and triploblastic - shared by many phyla (Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata larvae)
(B) Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, post-anal tail - these are the defining synapomorphies of Phylum Chordata
(C) Segmented body and appendages - found in Annelida and Arthropoda, not all chordates
(D) Deuterostome development - shared with Echinodermata and Hemichordata
Step 2: Only option B lists features unique to and diagnostic of chordates.
Why others are wrong: (A), (C), and (D) are either not unique to chordates or not present in all chordates.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The graph shows the trend in the ratio of gametophyte (n) to sporophyte (2n) dominance across plant evolution from algae to angiosperms. Which curve correctly represents this evolutionary trend?
options: U-shaped curve with equal dominance at both ends
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze evolutionary trend in plant life cycles:
• Algae: Haplontic - gametophyte dominant, sporophyte reduced
• Bryophytes: Gametophyte dominant, sporophyte dependent
• Pteridophytes: Sporophyte dominant, gametophyte independent but reduced
• Gymnosperms & Angiosperms: Sporophyte highly dominant, gametophyte extremely reduced (dependent)
Step 2: The evolutionary trend shows increasing sporophyte dominance and decreasing gametophyte dominance - a decreasing ratio of gametophyte to sporophyte dominance.
Why others are wrong: (A) Opposite of actual trend; (C) Ratio changes significantly; (D) No U-shaped pattern exists.
questions.imagePrompt: A line graph with Y-axis labeled 'Gametophyte Dominance (relative to Sporophyte)' from high (100%) to low (0%), and X-axis showing evolutionary progression: Algae → Bryophytes → Pteridophytes → Gymnosperms → Angiosperms. Curve starts high (Algae), gradually decreases through Bryophytes, drops more steeply at Pteridophytes, and approaches near-zero for Gymnosperms and Angiosperms. Clean scientific graph with trend line and labeled plant groups.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is a defining feature of class Mammalia but NOT found in class Aves (birds)?
options: Presence of diaphragm and milk-producing mammary glands
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Compare mammals and birds:
(A) Both are homeothermic (warm-blooded)
(B) Both have four-chambered hearts (complete double circulation)
(C) Diaphragm (muscular partition for breathing) and mammary glands (milk production) - these are unique to mammals
(D) Both are vertebrates with vertebrae and cranium
Step 2: Only option C lists features found exclusively in mammals.
Why others are wrong: (A), (B), and (D) are shared characteristics of both mammals and birds.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A student discovers a heterotrophic organism that is eukaryotic, unicellular, has chitinous cell walls, and reproduces by budding and spore formation. It lacks chlorophyll and is saprophytic. This organism belongs to kingdom:
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze the characteristics:
• Heterotrophic, saprophytic - obtains nutrition from dead organic matter
• Eukaryotic, unicellular - has membrane-bound nucleus
• Chitinous cell walls - nitrogen-containing polysaccharide
• Reproduces by budding and spores - asexual reproduction methods
• No chlorophyll - non-photosynthetic
Step 2: These are defining characteristics of Kingdom Fungi (specifically yeasts which are unicellular fungi).
Why others are wrong: (A) Protista - cell walls not chitinous (if present); (C) Monera - prokaryotic, peptidoglycan cell walls; (D) Plantae - photosynthetic, cellulose cell walls.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The diagram shows a cross-section of a Gram-positive bacterial cell wall. Which labeled component is responsible for retaining the crystal violet dye during Gram staining?
options: Thick peptidoglycan layer with teichoic acids
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Gram staining mechanism:
• Crystal violet dye enters all bacterial cells
• Iodine acts as mordant, forms complex with dye
• Decolorization step: Alcohol/acetone washes away dye from Gram-negative bacteria
• Gram-positive bacteria retain dye because of their thick peptidoglycan layer (20-80 nm) which traps the crystal violet-iodine complex
• Teichoic acids in Gram-positive cell walls also help retain stain
Step 2: Thick peptidoglycan layer is responsible for Gram-positive retention of crystal violet.
Why others are wrong: (A) LPS is in Gram-negative outer membrane; (B) Thin peptidoglycan is Gram-negative, doesn't retain dye; (D) Periplasmic space is not involved in dye retention.
questions.imagePrompt: A diagram showing cross-section of Gram-positive bacterial cell wall. Labels pointing to: (A) Lipopolysaccharide layer, (B) Thin peptidoglycan layer, (C) Thick peptidoglycan layer with teichoic acids (shown as dense mesh), (D) Periplasmic space, (E) Plasma membrane, (F) Cytoplasm. Crystal violet dye molecules shown trapped in thick peptidoglycan layer (C). Comparison with thin layer (B) showing dye washed away. Microscopic diagram style.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following represents the correct sequence of increasing complexity/organization in biological systems?
options: Atom → Molecule → Organelle → Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism
Molecule → Atom → Cell → Organelle → Tissue → Organ → Organism
Atom → Molecule → Cell → Organelle → Tissue → Organ → Organ system
Cell → Organelle → Molecule → Atom → Tissue → Organ → Organism
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Biological organization follows hierarchical levels from simple to complex:
Atomic level → Molecular level → Organelle level (within cells) → Cellular level → Tissue level (group of similar cells) → Organ level (different tissues) → Organ system level (organs working together) → Organism level
Step 2: Option A shows the correct ascending order of biological complexity.
Why others are wrong: (B) Atom is simpler than molecule, organelle is within cell; (C) Organelle is within cell, not after; (D) Completely reversed order.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The diagram shows a comparison of floral structures in two families: Solanaceae and Fabaceae. Based on the morphological features shown, which statement correctly distinguishes them?
options: Both families have zygomorphic flowers and diadelphous stamens
Solanaceae has actinomorphic flowers with fused petals and monadelphous stamens; Fabaceae has zygomorphic flowers with papilionaceous corolla and diadelphous stamens
Both families have actinomorphic flowers with free petals and polyadelphous stamens
Fabaceae has actinomorphic flowers with radial symmetry; Solanaceae has zygomorphic flowers with bilateral symmetry
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze family characteristics from diagram:
Solanaceae (e.g., tomato, potato, petunia):
• Actinomorphic (radially symmetrical) flowers
• 5 fused petals (gamopetalous)
• 5 stamens, often monadelphous (united by filaments) or free
Fabaceae (Leguminosae, e.g., pea, bean):
• Zygomorphic (bilaterally symmetrical) flowers
• Papilionaceous corolla: standard (large upper), two wings, two fused keels
• 10 stamens, often diadelphous (9 united + 1 free)
Step 2: Option B correctly describes these distinguishing features.
Why others are wrong: (A) Solanaceae is actinomorphic, not zygomorphic; (C) Both have different symmetry; (D) Reversed - Fabaceae is zygomorphic, Solanaceae is actinomorphic.
questions.imagePrompt: A comparative diagram showing floral structures of two families side by side. Left: Solanaceae flower - radially symmetric (actinomorphic), 5 fused petals forming star/bell shape, 5 stamens with united filaments (monadelphous). Right: Fabaceae flower - bilaterally symmetric (zygomorphic), papilionaceous structure with large upper standard petal, two lateral wings, two lower petals fused into keel, 10 stamens showing diadelphous arrangement (9 fused + 1 free). Labels for all parts. Botanical illustration style.
